title: Brave New World
synopsis: World State, six hundred years on. Ford bless us. The soma is free. The conditioning is finished by age six. You're an Alpha-Plus, slightly maladjusted, slightly too much.

nodes.text: You are walked past the fertilizing room, the bottle racks, and the Social Predestination Room, and everyone around you takes notes because it will be on the exam. Bokanovsky's Process: one egg, ninety-six identical humans, a major instrument of social stability. The bottles crawl by at thirty-three centimetres an hour. Someone asks how many, and the answer comes back in tonnes. Everyone nods. You nod.

choices.consequence: You nod at the correct intervals and ask the question the Director is hoping for. It costs nothing and buys two more years of being left alone.
You notice that stability gets described as both an achievement and an inevitability, and that nobody has ever needed both words at once.

nodes.text: Eight-month-old Deltas are set down among roses and picture books, and reach for them, and receive a shock through the floor while sirens go off. Two hundred repetitions. They will hate flowers and books instinctively for eighty years and never once know why. Then the sleep-teaching: a soft voice under the pillow, sixty-two thousand repetitions — which is not education but the manufacture of preference.

choices.consequence: Something in you objects, quietly, and has no vocabulary whatsoever to object with. That part is by design.
You laugh at the babies, because it is funny, because it is meant to be, and because laughing is the cheapest exit available.

nodes.text: Lenina Crowne is pneumatic, cheerful, universally liked, and mildly scandalous for having gone four months with the same man. She asks you to a feely — a picture where you hold the knobs and feel the bearskin rug on your own skin along with everyone else in the theatre. And soma afterward, obviously. Half a gramme is a half-holiday. A gramme is better.

choices.consequence: You go, and it is genuinely lovely, and you take the soma, and the evening closes over the top of you like warm water.
You say no, and she looks at you the way one looks at a stain, and word is round the department inside a day.

nodes.text: Helmholtz Watson writes emotional engineering slogans and lectures at the College of Writers, is very good at both, and is quietly dying of it. He has far too much ability and nothing on Earth to spend it on. He wants to write something piercing — he uses the word x-rayish — and cannot, because in a world with no loss in it there is nothing to be piercing about.

choices.consequence: You find, alarmingly, that you can say things to him you have never said aloud to anybody, and that he says them straight back.
You keep it professional, because friendship with a marked man is itself a mark, and you are already very slightly the wrong shape for your caste.

nodes.text: Bernard Marx is an Alpha with the body of a Gamma and a rumour about alcohol in his blood-surrogate, and he has built an entire personality out of resenting both. He talks about being himself, alone, seriously — which is impressive until you notice he only ever says it to people who cannot report him. He is not brave. He is unpopular, and he has confused the two.

choices.consequence: He has a permit for the Reservation and needs a witness, and you agree, and you both pretend it is friendship.
You put distance between you, which is sensible and slightly shameful, and he notices at once because he always notices.

nodes.text: Malpais, behind sixty thousand kilometres of electrified fence: dust, dogs, a drum going since before dawn, an old man with no teeth, women who gave birth to their own children. A boy is whipped around the plaza until his back opens and he does not cry out, and the crowd is not appalled, because this is worship. And there is a young man watching who is blond, blue-eyed, and speaking English out of Shakespeare.

choices.consequence: You realise on the flight home that you are carrying a person the way one carries a specimen, and you do it anyway.
You leave him where he belongs, which is a place that does not want him either, and which is the more honest cruelty.

nodes.text: John's mother was a Beta on holiday twenty years ago, left behind after a fall in a storm, and she has aged in a place with no youth treatments, no soma, and no way home. She is enormous and toothless and reeks of mescal, and she is overjoyed to see people from civilization, and what she wants to talk about is zippers. The village despises her. The man who left her is now the Director.

choices.consequence: She is proof, and proof is a weapon, and you can watch Bernard working out precisely where to aim it.
You leave her to the mescal and the village women. John will not forgive it, and neither, eventually, will you.

nodes.text: The Director is destroyed in public in roughly ninety seconds — a fat old woman calling him her lover in front of the entire Hatchery — and Bernard, who arranged all of it, is suddenly the most sought-after man in London. Everyone wants the Savage at their party. Bernard supplies him. He is smug, expansive, sleeping with six different women, and he has never once asked John whether he minds.

choices.consequence: You start refusing invitations on John's behalf, lose a great many of your own, and gain the only thing in this city worth having.
You watch a man be converted into an entertainment and tell yourself it is not your business, which is true, and no defence at all.

nodes.text: Lenina wants him, which in her world is a simple, hygienic, entirely respectable thing to want. She takes her clothes off and says so plainly. And John — who learned love out of a battered Shakespeare and has been worshipping her as something to be earned across years — hears it as filth, calls her a strumpet, and comes within an inch of striking her. Neither of them has done anything wrong.

choices.consequence: You try explaining each of them to the other and discover no words exist in either vocabulary. That is the entire problem, standing in one room.
You leave them to it. She locks herself in the bathroom and he stands outside the door shouting scripture through it.

nodes.text: The Hospital for the Dying is bright and warm and smells of synthetic musk, with a television at the foot of every bed. Linda has been on a soma holiday for weeks and it is now killing her precisely on schedule. John holds her hand and she surfaces once and calls him by another man's name. Around the bed, a Bokanovsky group of eight-year-old twins is being death-conditioned with chocolate éclairs.

choices.consequence: You stand with him while the children ask what is wrong with her, and you have no answer that is not an obscenity.
You leave before the end, and you will never be able to say afterward whether that was tact or cowardice.

nodes.text: He comes out of the hospital straight into the soma distribution — a hundred and sixty-two Deltas queued for their ration — and something in him finally lets go. He tells them they are free, that the ration is poison, that they are men, and they look back at him with no comprehension whatsoever. So he goes to the window and starts throwing the boxes out into the yard, handful after handful.

choices.consequence: You get to the window and start throwing with him, and it is exhilarating and entirely futile and the best thing you have ever done.
You stay by the door with your hands at your sides. It is the correct assessment of the situation, and it will sit in you for decades.

nodes.text: The riot police arrive with soma vapour, water pistols full of anaesthetic, and the Synthetic Anti-Riot Speech, Number Two, played at medium strength. Inside four minutes the Deltas are weeping and kissing one another and apologising. Nobody is beaten. Nobody is arrested. It is the gentlest suppression imaginable, and it is total, and that is exactly why it never has to happen twice.

choices.consequence: You shout over the Voice, and the Voice is louder and kinder and far better engineered, and the crowd hears it instead.
You get behind a pillar and watch order restored by a recording, which is somehow more frightening than truncheons would have been.

nodes.text: Mustapha Mond, Resident Controller for Western Europe, keeps a safe full of forbidden books and reads them, and is one of perhaps ten people alive permitted to. He is charming. He agrees with almost everything John says. Yes, it is shallow. Yes, art and science and God were the price. Yes, he knows exactly what was traded away — and he would make the same trade again tomorrow, for reasons he lays out so well you cannot answer them.

choices.consequence: You claim the right to be unhappy, to have cancer, to be afraid of tomorrow — and he grants all of it immediately and without a fight, which is worse than refusal.
You let him finish. Every sentence is reasonable. You understand for the first time that this world was built by people who had thought about it much harder than you have.

nodes.text: Bernard hears the word island and goes to pieces on the carpet — pleading, weeping, blaming John and Helmholtz by name, offering anything at all. They carry him out and dose him. He gets Iceland. What he never grasps, even at the end, is that exile is not the punishment: the islands are where they put the interesting people, and he is being sent somewhere he is not interesting enough for.

choices.consequence: You get him upright and cleaned up and talking, and he thanks you, and by morning he has decided the whole thing was your fault.
You let him fall apart alone, which he has largely earned, and which you will not enjoy remembering.

nodes.text: Helmholtz takes it standing up and asks one question: which island. He wants somewhere with bad weather. He believes he will write better in a gale, on the theory that a man needs something to push against and there has been nothing to push against his entire life. Mond, who came within one decision of being sent to an island himself, gives him the Falklands and looks almost wistful about it.

choices.consequence: He is being exiled into the only honest company left on the planet, and he knows it, and you would go tomorrow if they asked.
You think about the cold, the isolation, the empty page. He laughs at you, and he is right to.

nodes.text: He is not allowed an island. He is too useful as an experiment. So he takes an abandoned air-lighthouse on a hill between Puttenham and Elstead and tries to build a life out of nothing but work and prayer: a bow, arrows, a garden, a whip. He says he wants to be purified. What he wants is to be punished, and he has confused the two so completely that nobody could untangle it now.

choices.consequence: You make the trip out and he is glad to see you for about four minutes before the shame closes over him again.
You leave him his solitude, which is what he asked for, and which turns out to be the one thing nobody will let him keep.

nodes.text: A reporter finds him. Then a feely camera hidden in a tree. Then the picture goes out across the whole country — the Savage of Surrey, flogging himself on a hilltop — and by the following weekend there are coaches. They park at the bottom and climb up and call to him and ask him to do it again. He is not a hermit any more. He is an attraction with a car park.

choices.consequence: You stand at the bottom of the hill turning back whoever you can, and for every one you turn back three more arrive with a picnic.
You stay at the edge with the rest of them, which makes you one of them, which is precisely what you came out here to prove you were not.

nodes.text: Lenina steps down out of a helicopter into the middle of it with her arms open, and he goes at her with the whip, and the crowd — who came for exactly this and did not know it — begins to chant. Then somebody starts singing. Then the soma comes out. The flogging becomes the dance becomes the thing every one of them was conditioned into at twelve years old, and he goes down into it with them.

choices.consequence: You wade in and get one hand on him and are swallowed by the same crowd, and you wake in the heather at dawn with no idea what you did.
You stand outside the ring of it and watch a man lose the last thing he had, and you do not move one step.

nodes.text: You come back up the hill at midday. The coaches are gone, the heather is trampled flat, there is rubbish in the gorse and a paper cup in the garden he planted. The lighthouse door stands open. Inside, in the archway at the top of the stairs, a pair of feet hangs and turns slowly to the right, then pauses, then turns slowly to the left, like two unhurried compass needles.

choices.consequence: You find a knife and do the necessary thing yourself, badly, and you are still doing it when the first camera crew arrives.
You stand at the bottom of the stairs and cannot make yourself climb them, and afterward you cannot say how long you were there.

nodes.text: Mond sends for you and is, as ever, perfectly pleasant about it. He has read your file. He observes that you were present at the Reservation, present at the riot, and present at the lighthouse, which is a very great deal of presence for one Alpha-Plus. Then he asks, with no threat in it whatsoever, whether you might prefer an island — and makes it sound like a favour, because it is one.

choices.consequence: You say it before you have finished deciding, and hearing your own voice say it is the first genuinely free moment of your life.
You decline, and he nods, and he does not send you anyway — which means you will now live the rest of it having chosen this.

nodes.text: A small town on a black shore under a sky that is doing something different every twenty minutes. No soma. No feelies. No Voice. Two hundred people who were all sent here for being too much, arguing loudly in a canteen about things that cannot be settled. It is cold, and dull, and difficult, and nobody has decided in advance what you are for.

choices.consequence: You spend a month doing nothing but walking the shore and letting the weather happen to you, and something in your chest slowly unclenches.
You start making notes on the second night, badly, in a hand you have not used since school.
There is a hill in Surrey with an empty building on it and nobody has claimed it, and it has been sitting at the back of your mind since the day you left.

nodes.text: You write a pamphlet about feeling — not an argument, just a plain description of what it is like to be sad on purpose, and to want something you cannot simply be handed. It is clumsy. It is also the only document of its kind. Copies go back to the mainland in the mail sacks and pass hand to hand among Alphas who read them once, late, alone, and put them straight into the incinerator, and cannot afterward stop thinking about them.

You take the transfer to the Falklands and find Helmholtz in a stone house with a stove and no curtains, and he has been writing for eleven years about wind, and solitude, and the particular quality of light before a storm. Nobody on Earth needs one word of it. He reads it aloud to you and to a cold sea, and you understand that this is what he was for the entire time, and that the world he came from would have killed him slowly, with comfort.

You take over the lighthouse. You burn the coins the tourists left in the grass and pull the rubbish out of the gorse and finish the garden he started. His books are still on the shelf with his notes crowded into the margins in a hand you come to know very well. You read all of them, alone, through one long wet winter — and then in spring you begin, slowly and with no certainty whatsoever, to decide what to do next.
